constitutive_assumptions: Multilayer structure represented as multiple elastic thin shells satisfying the Kirchhoff-Love hypothesis
Continuous displacement field constructed by extracting mid-plane displacements across turns based on deformation similarity
Neglect of induced electromotive force generated by current along the tape width (tape width inductance omitted)
Axial velocity assumed to be zero in time derivative of mutual inductance, retaining only radial velocity
Turn-to-turn mechanical separation neglected due to a 0.5 mm outer overband suppressing separation
Radial contact resistance varies solely due to deformation-induced changes in geometrical contact area, omitting contact pressure, preload, surface condition, and inter-turn friction
Normal layer treated with constant equivalent resistivity in parallel with the superconducting layer
Power-law E-J constitutive relation for superconducting resistive voltage
Linear elastic mechanical constitutive behavior with orthotropic/transversely isotropic equivalent elastic moduli and Poisson ratios
control_variables: Coil dimensions: 48 turns, inner diameter 25 mm, tape width 4 mm, tape thickness 0.1 mm, overband thickness 0.5 mm
Superconducting tape self-field critical current Ic0 at 4.2 K: 2120 A
Equivalent radial contact resistivity rho_r: 1.6 micro-ohm*cm^2 for NI coil (1 ohm*m^2 for insulated comparison)
Equivalent mechanical parameters: Er = 134 GPa, Ephi = 144 GPa, Ez = 144 GPa; Grphi = 48 GPa, Gphiz = 55 GPa, Grz = 48 GPa; Poisson ratios nurphi = 0.314, nuphiz = 0.3, nurz = 0.314
ODE solver tolerances: absolute and relative tolerances set to 1e-4
dependent_variables: Azimuthal current distribution and screening current density
Radial current and radial current density distribution
Inductance matrix coefficients and time derivative of mutual inductance
Displacement fields (radial ur and axial uz) and rotation angle alpha
Hoop strain distribution and maximum hoop strain
Azimuthal magnetization loss power and power density
Radial Joule heating loss power and power density

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: A multilayer structural continuum model based on elastic thin shells satisfying the Kirchhoff-Love hypothesis was formulated to model coil deformation and interfacial slip under non-uniform electromagnetic forces.

The coupled electromagnetic-mechanical model predicts hoop strain difference with a 15.5% relative error against experimental measurements on a 3-turn REBCO coil under a 3.52 T field, compared to 70% error for an uncoupled model.
Deformation-induced rotation alters local perpendicular and parallel field components, mitigating critical current degradation and altering the mechanical strain evolution.
Electromechanical coupling suppresses maximum hoop strain from 0.457% to 0.35% during initial excitation, but amplifies maximum hoop strain from 0.456% to 0.481% after stabilization.
The study focuses strictly on high-temperature superconducting magnet coils and does not evaluate soft robotics, continuum robots, soft grippers, or variable stiffness mechanisms.

experimental_setup: Validation against experimental strain difference measurements from literature (Li et al., 2020) for a 3-turn REBCO insulated coil under axial magnetic fields up to 3.52 T
Numerical benchmark comparison with a 2D axisymmetric finite-element T-A formulation model under an external magnetic field ramp to 12 T and coil charging to 500 A
future_work: Incorporating a more detailed contact resistance description that accounts for local contact pressure, preload, surface condition, and inter-turn sliding
independent_variables: Time during external field magnetization ramp, stabilization hold, and coil charging
External magnetic field magnitude and ramp rate (up to 12 T)
Inserted coil operating current and charging rate (ramped to 500 A at 5 A/s)
Power-law index n-value (varied to test sensitivity)
Coupling mechanism modes (uncoupled, critical current effect only, inductance effect included, contact resistance effect included)
Radial and axial positions within the coil (turn number and height along tape width)
limitations_inferred: Thermal coupling is omitted; the coil is assumed isothermal at 4.2 K despite computed radial Joule heating and azimuthal magnetization losses, preventing thermal feedback into material properties.
The 2D axisymmetric formulation cannot model three-dimensional non-axisymmetric phenomena such as tape joints, localized defects, or non-uniform winding geometry.
The methodology was not applied to or evaluated on soft robots, continuum manipulators, soft grippers, or robotic variable-stiffness devices.
limitations_stated_by_authors: The model adopts simplifications and does not capture practical details such as REBCO tape composite structure and inter-tape frictional behavior (Page 7).
Tape non-uniformities along length and width (such as local critical current variations) are not fully accounted for (Page 7).

Experimental validation was restricted to a 3-turn insulated coil without radial current paths, validating only steady-state strain without verifying transient radial current dynamics of NI coils (Pages 7-8).
The contact resistance model considers only geometric contact area variations from deformation, omitting local contact pressure, preload, surface conditions, and inter-turn sliding (Page 4).
Axial velocity is assumed to be zero in the mutual inductance time derivative to reduce computational complexity (Page 4).
Induced electromotive force generated by current along the tape width is neglected (Page 2).
main_results: The artificial neural network (ANN) calculates inductance coefficients with a maximum relative error of 0.01% and reduces computation time from 10,199 s to approximately 0.02 s per evaluation.
The coupled model achieves a relative error of 15.5% against experimental strain difference data under a 3.52 T field, outperforming the uncoupled model error of 70%.
Electromechanical coupling intensifies radial current bypass during coil charging and increases radial current density, especially in outermost turns.
Mechanical deflection modifies local field components, mitigating critical current degradation and causing shallower screening current penetration depth with higher peak azimuthal current density.
Coupling suppresses maximum hoop strain from 0.457% to 0.35% in early excitation stages but amplifies it from 0.456% to 0.481% after the system stabilizes.
The coupled model predicts higher local peak azimuthal magnetization loss power density and increased radial Joule heating loss compared to the uncoupled model.
Deformation-induced inductance variation is the dominant mechanism driving changes in radial current and shielding current distribution.
Higher power-law n-values increase the shielding current density concentration at coil ends, leading to increased local hoop strain.
modeling_methods: Axisymmetric partial element equivalent circuit (A-PEEC) model based on Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws
Multilayer structural continuum mechanics model based on elastic thin shell theory satisfying the Kirchhoff-Love hypothesis and incorporating interfacial slip
Artificial neural network (ANN) with dual hidden layers to compute quadruple integrals for mutual and self-inductance from the Neumann formula
Split-field iteration method coupling the circuit model in MATLAB (ode15s) with COMSOL finite-element magnetic and mechanical solvers
Power-law E-J relation for superconducting resistive voltage and magnetic vector potential (A-formulation) for magnetic field solution
Deformation-dependent critical current model incorporating magnetic field angle deflection and hoop strain degradation
performance_metrics: Inductance evaluation computation time: approximately 0.02 s (ANN) vs. 10,199 s (numerical integration)
Inductance coefficient relative error: maximum error <= 0.01%
Relative error in strain difference compared to experimental data: 15.5% (coupled) vs. 70% (uncoupled)
Maximum hoop strain suppression/amplification: 0.35% vs. 0.457% (early stage) and 0.481% vs. 0.456% (steady state)
Split-field convergence iterations per time step: typically 3 to 5 iterations
Loss power magnitudes: azimuthal magnetization loss power and radial Joule heating loss power
possible_gap_implications: The coupled continuum mechanics and electromagnetic circuit modeling approach could offer insights for modeling electromechanically active flexible structures, though adapting it to soft robotics would require large-strain kinematics and multi-material hyperelasticity.
Using neural networks to accelerate deformation-dependent electromagnetic integrals could be adapted to real-time control or simulation of magnetically actuated soft or continuum devices.
The omission of thermal feedback and contact friction indicates that comprehensive multiphysics modeling remains a challenge when simulating flexible electromagnetic mechanisms.
paper.research_objective: To develop an electromagnetic-mechanical bidirectional coupled numerical model for high-temperature superconducting no-insulation coils based on an ANN-accelerated circuit model and split-field iteration method, and to systematically analyze the multiphysics response (electromagnetic, mechanical, and loss behavior).
paper.research_problem: In high-temperature superconducting (HTS) no-insulation (NI) coils, shielding currents create non-uniform electromagnetic forces causing mechanical deformation, which in turn alters coil inductance and tape critical current; however, repeatedly recalculating the inductance matrix in coupled circuit models is computationally prohibitive using conventional numerical integration.
paper.title: A coupled electromagnetic-mechanical model for high temperature superconducting coils based on circuit model
